title: Performance Engineering & Profiling
summary: Your intuition about what's slow is wrong more often than it's right. This is the discipline of measuring where time actually goes, then fixing the part that matters.

blocks.markdown:
Performance engineering is one loop: measure, find the biggest cost, fix it, verify, repeat.

- **The golden rule: measure, don't guess.** Profile first; your gut about the hot spot is usually wrong.
- Most runtime lives in a tiny fraction of the code — optimizing blindly wastes weeks polishing code that barely runs.
- Modern cost is invisible: cache misses, locks, GC, network waits. Only instruments see the waiting.
- The skill isn't cleverness; it's the discipline to look before you cut.

blocks.subTitle: Symptom to tool
blocks.markdown:
Match the symptom to the right move before reaching for any tool.

| Symptom | Reach for |
|---|---|
| One request is slow | Latency profiling + flame graph |
| Maxes out under load | Throughput test + USE method |
| Slow but CPU idle | I/O wait, locks, GC pauses |
| p99 bad, p50 fine | Tail: timeouts, hedging, isolation |

blocks.subTitle: Latency, throughput, utilization
blocks.markdown:
Three metrics that get confused constantly — pin them down.

- **Latency** — time for one unit of work. "This call took 80ms." Lower is better.
- **Throughput** — units per unit time. "5,000 requests/second." Higher is better.
- **Utilization** — fraction of a resource in use. "CPU at 85%."

They fight each other. Batching raises throughput but adds latency. Pushing utilization toward 100% forms queues, so latency shoots toward infinity — keep latency-sensitive systems below ~70-80%.

blocks.subTitle: Profilers: sampling vs instrumentation
blocks.markdown:
A profiler tells you where time or memory goes. Two ways to gather it.

- **Sampling** — interrupt the program ~100-1000x/sec and record the call stack. Cheap (few % overhead), statistical, safe in production. The function in the most samples is the hot spot.
- **Instrumentation** — time every function entry/exit. Exact counts, but high overhead and it distorts what you measure (observer effect).
- Rule: **sample to find the problem, instrument only when you need exact call counts.**

blocks.subTitle: Reading a flame graph
blocks.markdown:
A flame graph turns thousands of stack samples into one readable picture.

- Each box is a function; a box sits on top of its caller (the stack).
- **Width** = total time in that function and its children. It is **not** a timeline — the x-axis is not time-ordered.
- Read it by scanning for the **widest boxes**, especially the widest **leaf** (top edge), because that's code actually burning CPU rather than waiting on a child.
- The widest top edge is your hot path to attack first.

blocks.subTitle: Amdahl's law
blocks.markdown:
Amdahl's law bounds how much a partial speedup can help.

- If fraction **p** of total time is the part you optimize, and you speed it up by factor **s**: total speedup = 1 / ((1−p) + p/s).
- Punchline: if p is just 5%, even making that part infinitely fast caps your total gain at ~5%.
- So **always optimize the biggest slice**, and notice when the remaining time is dominated by parts you can't easily speed up.

blocks.subTitle: Tail latency & the USE method
blocks.markdown:
Averages hide pain; the unlucky 1% is what users feel.

- Track **percentiles** — p50, p95, p99, p99.9 — not the mean. A great average can hide a terrible p99.
- **Fan-out amplifies it:** if one request triggers 100 backend calls and waits for all, the chance at least one hits the slow 1% is ~63% — rare slowness becomes the common case.
- **USE method** finds the bottleneck resource fast: check **U**tilization, **S**aturation (queued work), **E**rrors. Highly utilized *and* saturated = your bottleneck.

blocks.subTitle: Fixes ranked by payoff
blocks.markdown:
Reach for the top of this list first — higher items give order-of-magnitude wins.

- **Better algorithm / data structure** — change the big-O (O(n²)→O(n log n)).
- **Caching** — avoid repeating identical work ([b05-caching](b05-caching.md)).
- **Batching** — amortize per-call overhead (N+1 → one query).
- **Connection pooling** — skip setup cost.
- **Async / parallelism** — overlap waiting.
- **Fewer allocations** — cut GC pressure (constant-factor win).

blocks.subTitle: What you're trading
blocks.markdown:
Every optimization spends something. Choose by what users feel.

- **Latency vs throughput** — batching and high utilization help throughput, hurt latency. Interactive paths protect latency; bulk pipelines maximize throughput.
- **Speed vs memory** — caching and precomputation spend RAM to save CPU, until memory pressure causes GC churn.
- **Speed vs complexity** — a clever lock-free structure is fast but easy to get subtly wrong. Simple-and-correct often beats fast-and-buggy.
- **Effort vs payoff** — bounded by Amdahl: 2x on a 50% slice beats 100x on a 1% slice.

blocks.subTitle: Worked example: N+1 query
blocks.markdown:
An endpoint's p99 is 1,400ms against a 200ms SLO. Walk the loop.

A p99 trace shows `db: fetch items` is 1,180ms — 85% of the time. The query log reveals why:

```sql
-- runs once PER item in the order: 200 items = 200 queries
SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id = ?
```

That's the classic **N+1 query** — invisible on small orders, explosive on big ones, so only the tail is slow. Fix with one batched round trip:

```sql
SELECT * FROM items WHERE order_id IN (?, ...)
```

Re-measure: p99 drops to 170ms, meeting the SLO. Then **stop** — further work burns effort with no user benefit.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & monitoring
blocks.markdown:
The big ideas show up in the systems you use daily.

- **Google's hedged requests** — after the p95 deadline, send a duplicate to another replica and take the first reply; a little extra load buys a big p99 cut.
- **Netflix + Linux `perf`** — sampling profiling at the kernel level feeds always-on flame graphs across a huge fleet.
- **JVM HotSpot JIT** — compiles hot methods to native code, which is why benchmarks must warm up.
- **Monitor:** latency percentiles per endpoint, USE per resource, GC pause time, and a continuous profiler ([b14-observability](b14-observability.md)).

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"I know what's slow, I'll just fix it."** The data routinely surprises experienced engineers — profile first.
- **Optimizing a tiny slice.** Amdahl caps the win near that slice's share. Find the biggest slice first.
- **Reporting the average.** It hides the tail; report p50/p95/p99.
- **No warmup on a JIT runtime.** Early runs measure the interpreter and compiler, not steady state.
- **Dead-code elimination.** If a microbenchmark's result is unused, the compiler deletes it — consume the output.
- **Unrealistic test data.** Tiny datasets and single-threaded runs hide N+1 and contention.
